entry.englishMeaning: to give renewed energy, strength, or effectiveness to something
entry.coreIdea: Give something fresh energy or strength.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Figurative verb for giving an organization renewed energy or effectiveness, as if making it more alive.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Positive: the organization and community are expected to become stronger.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Motivational and confident here: mastering difficult discussions is promised to improve the wider community.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Formal and relatively uncommon. “Energize” is more familiar; do not label this word ordinary everyday speech.

when_to_use: Describe giving an organization, community or activity new energy and effectiveness.
when_not_to_use: In ordinary conversation, give new energy to is often clearer than vitalize. Do not use it simply to mean keep something unchanged.

advanced_nuance: Vitalize presents change as giving life or energy to something. Applied to an organization, it is figurative rather than a claim about a living body.
The source predicts a benefit from better discussions. Using vitalize does not itself prove that the benefit will occur.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture new volunteers bringing activity to a quiet community centre.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: New volunteers helped vitalize the community project.
memory_practice.production_task: Write one sentence using vitalize with the pattern “vitalize + organization, community, or activity.”
memory_practice.recall_question: What does vitalize mean in the source context?
memory_practice.recognition_task: One project gains new volunteers and useful ideas; another keeps its routine unchanged. Which change is more likely to vitalize the project?

examples.example_1: Open dialogue can vitalize an organization.
examples.example_2: New volunteers helped vitalize the community project.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: What could vitalize the community project?
B: New volunteers with time and ideas could help.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: As  you  and  others  master  high­ stakes  discussions,  you'll  also  vitalize  your  organization  and  your  community .
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to give renewed energy, strength, or effectiveness to something
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The writer says that improving difficult discussions will give the organization and community more energy and effectiveness.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: The new ideas could vitalize to the organization.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say The new ideas could vitalize the organization. Vitalize takes its object directly, without to.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Vitalize means give energy or strength. Maintain means keep something going; maintenance does not necessarily bring fresh energy.

entry.englishMeaning: to improve a skill or knowledge you learned before but have not used recently
entry.coreIdea: Picture brushing dust off a skill you already own.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Idiomatic phrasal verb for refreshing knowledge or a skill learned previously; here, French before a trip.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Constructive: it presents improvement as renewing an existing foundation.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Practical and purposeful here: the speaker links language revision to an upcoming trip.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Conversational, also natural among colleagues. It suggests prior learning, not starting from zero.

when_to_use: Describe a skill you want to refresh and a small practice plan.
A natural model: I need to brush up on my spreadsheet skills before the course.
when_not_to_use: For a subject you have never learned, say learn or start learning. Brush up on suggests some previous knowledge.

advanced_nuance: Brush up on suggests refreshing an existing foundation. It does not promise complete mastery or require that all earlier knowledge has been forgotten.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture brushing dust off a skill you already own.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: I need to brush up on my spreadsheet skills before the course.
memory_practice.production_task: Describe a skill you want to refresh and a small practice plan. Use the target expression in one or two sentences. Check its pattern and register only after speaking.
memory_practice.recall_question: Without looking, retrieve the expression meaning to improve a skill or knowledge you learned before but have not used recently. Then say it in a new situation.
memory_practice.recognition_task: Choose the natural sentence. A: I need to brush up on to write reports. B: I need to brush up on writing reports. Explain why, then check the correction after answering.

examples.scenario: I want to brush up on my French before the trip.
examples.another_setting: I need to brush up on my spreadsheet skills before the course.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: I need to brush up on my spreadsheet skills before the course.
B: There is a short practice session next week.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: I want to brush up on my French before the trip.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to improve a skill or knowledge you learned before but have not used recently
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speaker has learned some French before and wants to practise it again so it will be easier to use on the trip.

mistakes_differences.correction: Say I need to brush up on writing reports. After on, use a noun or an -ing form, not to + verb.
mistakes_differences.common_mistake: I need to brush up on to write reports.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Brushing up refreshes prior learning; starting from scratch introduces something entirely new.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: brush up on + subject/skill/noun or -ing form

entry.coreIdea: Close to a quantity, state or completion, without claiming exactness.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Approximation phrase meaning almost completely in this sentence: most packing is done, but some may remain.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: it deliberately avoids claiming full completion.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Informal and qualified here: the speaker gives a broadly positive update while leaving room for unfinished details.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common in conversation and informal updates. Specify the remaining work if the listener needs an exact status.

when_to_use: Give an approximate comparison or say something is nearly complete when exact precision is not needed.
when_not_to_use: When a precise amount or completion status matters, state it directly instead of relying on more or less.

advanced_nuance: More or less can describe approximate sameness or near completion. In the source, it means the packing is nearly finished.
The phrase does not tell the listener the size of the remaining gap. Add what is left when that detail affects a decision.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture a nearly packed suitcase with a few small items still beside it.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: The two routes take more or less the same time.
memory_practice.production_task: Give an honest near-completion update without claiming everything is finished. Respond in one or two natural sentences using the expression, then compare with the pattern after answering.
memory_practice.recall_question: Recall the expression for this meaning without looking: approximately or almost completely. Explain its function in one sentence.
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which option fits the taught meaning and standard construction? A: The routes take more or less the same time. B: The routes take more and less the same time. Explain your choice, then check the correction and distinction.

examples.scenario: We have more or less finished packing.
examples.another_setting: The two routes take more or less the same time.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: The two routes take more or less the same time.
B: Then let us choose the one with fewer changes.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: We have more or less finished packing.
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: Most of the packing is finished, but a few things may still need to be packed. The speaker does not claim that every item is ready.

mistakes_differences.correction: The routes take more or less the same time.
mistakes_differences.common_mistake: The routes take more and less the same time.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: More or less gives approximation; exactly claims precision.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: more or less + adjective/participle; more or less the same
